18:12 Local Time, 16:12 GMT, 21:42 IST: Scott Boland doing the damage again - two wickets yesterday and two today as South Africa find themselves on 97/5 as the players leave the field. Just relentless accuracy with his lines and lengths, while also finding more movement than anyone else. Mitchell Starc found better rhythm today and chipped in with a wicket as well. It took a long time for play to kick off on Day 2, but things happened quickly once the Aussies took the field. The pitch isn't offering extravagant movement, but Boland has just been in a league of his own so far. We're expecting better weather for the next three days. 09:00 Local Time, 07:00 GMT, 12:30 IST: Hello and welc... nah, forget that! Let’s get straight to the most important bit: what’s the weather like in Gqeberha right now? And we have a positive update from ground zero, courtesy of Telford Vice: “Morning! No rain overnight and a bright and beautiful morning. Should start on time.”

It has been a frustrating first two days at St George’s Park, with persistent rain and a soggy outfield wiping out around 137 overs and leaving this second Test looking more like a three-day contest. A result is still possible, though, and Australia are certainly better placed to push for a win, thanks in no small part to their super-sub Scott Boland. Losing so much time is disappointing and irritating, but we have at least been treated to 14 overs of pure bowling class from Boland across the first two days. He bowled Aiden Markram with a beauty that swung back in, had David Bedingham and Marques Ackerman caught behind, and then watched Matt Renshaw pull off a stunning one-handed catch at first slip to dismiss Ryan Rickelton. Boland has given Australia a genuine chance of going for that win, and they will be eager to make it count.

Temba Bavuma has been a rock for South Africa, but the hosts have plenty of work to do. If Australia can wrap up the South African innings in the first session today, they could still have enough time to force a result. They would then need to score quickly and give their bowlers enough overs to bowl South Africa out again. The Proteas, meanwhile, face a much steeper climb. They may need inspiration from Australia’s performance in the first Test, when Renshaw and the lower order lifted their side from 124/6 to 390. If Bavuma and the lower order can produce something similar, South Africa could put Australia under some pressure, especially with Kagiso Rabada back in the attack. However, they first need to post a decent first-innings total. But with so little time left, scoring enough to give themselves a realistic chance of bowling Australia out twice will be extremely difficult. Of course, all of this hinges on one crucial factor: the weather.
